title: each as a lens for a week
word: each as a lens for a week
hook: a rumor at the bus stop and a friend who snaps at you: the first two lenses, Nyaya and Vaisheshika, on an ordinary day
carry: each as a lens for a week
tomorrow: each as a lens for a week

segments.voice: Yesterday we began each as a lens for a week: six schools, six questions, clicked in like lenses at the eye doctor. Which question did you ask of something annoying? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-eight.

Eight in the morning, at the bus stop. A neighbor leans over and says the bakery on the corner is closing for good. She heard it from her cousin. By lunch, it's all up and down the street. Later that afternoon, a friend snaps at you over something small, and a thought can stick for the rest of the day: so that's who they really are. Two ordinary moments. In both, something was taken as known a little too fast. Today we click in the first pair of lenses, the two schools that tradition studies together, Nyaya and Vaisheshika, and look again.
screen: `THE BAKERY IS CLOSING.` → `A FRIEND SNAPS.` → `KNOWN A LITTLE TOO FAST.`

segments.voice: First, the Nyaya lens. Its question: how do I know? The Nyaya Sutra names the means of right knowing: perception, inference, comparison, and the word of a reliable person. Click that lens onto the bus stop. Did anyone see a sign on the bakery's door? That would be perception. Is someone reasoning from empty shelves? That's inference, and Nyaya tests it. Or is it testimony? Then the question becomes whose. The Sutra says the word that counts is the word of a reliable person, someone who knows and tells it straight. A cousin of a neighbor, unchecked, isn't that yet. Under this lens, the rumor doesn't become false. It just becomes not yet known. Now the Vaisheshika lens. Its question: what is this made of? We met its list earlier in this part: substance, quality, action, and more. Click it onto your friend. There's the person, the substance. There's the irritation, a quality, passing through. There's the snapping, an action, a single movement that came and went. Vaisheshika keeps those apart on purpose. A quality lives in a thing; it isn't the thing. An action happens to a thing; it doesn't define it. So the thought, that's who they really are, turns out to be a category mistake. You took a quality for the substance. These two lenses are cool and patient. They slow down the leap. That's why tradition pairs them. One checks how you know. The other checks what you're looking at.
screen: `NYAYA: HOW DO I KNOW?` · `WHOSE WORD IS IT?` · `VAISHESHIKA: WHAT IS THIS MADE OF?` · `A MOOD IS NOT A PERSON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: use both lenses on one thing you believe about someone. Settle, and let a recent impression of a person come to mind. First, the Nyaya lens: how do I know this? Did I see it, reason to it, or hear it from someone? Just notice which. Then the Vaisheshika lens: is this the person, or a quality passing through them, or one action that came and went? Let the person stay whole while the mood and the moment fall into their places. Then rest. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Each as a lens for a week. Today, the first pair: Nyaya asks how do I know, Vaisheshika asks what is this made of. Today's word.
screen: `EACH AS A LENS FOR A WEEK — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: each as a lens for a week. Today, before you pass along a piece of news, ask: did someone see this, or did someone just say it? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Nyaya and Vaisheshika are traditionally studied together, and students of Indian logic learn the Nyaya Sutra's means of knowing alongside Vaisheshika's categories of what there is.

match.prompt: the first pair of lenses — tap the pairs.

myth: for Nyaya, any testimony counts as knowledge
the Sutra counts the word of a reliable person, someone who knows and tells it straight.
Vaisheshika keeps a thing apart from its qualities and actions
a quality lives in a thing, but it isn't the thing.
under the Nyaya lens, an unchecked rumor becomes false

fork.setup: a friend snaps at you. you're looking through the Vaisheshika lens. what do you see?
options: the friend's true character, finally showing.
a person, a passing quality, and one action.
fork.reveal: Vaisheshika keeps substance, quality and action apart, so one mood doesn't become the whole person.

original.note: Sanskrit: a means of right knowing, the heart of the Nyaya lens.

trapdoor: what you thought: logic and atoms are dry topics with nothing to say about a bad day.
what it means: Nyaya asks how you know, Vaisheshika asks what you're looking at, and together they slow the leap to conclusions.
what a scholar hears: Nyaya Sutra 1.1.3 and 1.1.7 on the pramanas and reliable testimony, with Vaisheshika Sutra 1.1.4's categories of substance, quality and action.
recall: stilling the movements of the mind

sources.ref: Nyaya Sutra 1.1.3 (perception, inference, comparison and word as the means of knowing)
Nyaya Sutra 1.1.7 (word as the teaching of a reliable person)
Vaisheshika Sutra 1.1.4 (substance, quality, action and the other categories)

notes: Nyaya Sutra 1.1.3 lists four pramanas; the script lists them without stating the count. Nyaya Sutra 1.1.7 defines shabda as the instruction of an apta (reliable person); confirm the paraphrase.
Vaisheshika Sutra 1.1.4's list of categories (numbering differs between recensions); the script names only substance, quality and action 'and more'. Confirm.
Applying the categories to a person's mood (quality vs. substance) is the course's own illustration, not a classical example. Confirm it doesn't distort the school.
'We met its list earlier in this part' refers to days 1166–1170; adjust if the schedule changes.
